details:
Micor Field / Martian OS is a Mars mission planning and exploration project built around a software simulation using real NASA data. It brings together an Earth and Mars clock and a set of mission modules: a Jezero map with route planning and EVA time budgeting, a tag-based digital logbook, and a rover-exploration view. The map and EVA planning are designed to help users compare fast and safer walking routes, select scientific stops, and consider the time needed for the excursion and return. The EVA budget is explicitly a lunar-analogue planning scenario not a validated Mars operational standard.

The simulation uses documented planetary datasets, including a Mars 2020 Terrain Relative Navigation HiRISE digital terrain model for Jezero (500 × 500 cells at 4 m per cell), ChemCam records from Glen Torridon, and MOLA topography. These datasets provide real scientific and terrain context for exploring routes and mission objectives. The rover module currently presents a Jezero orthophoto; it should not be described as an interactive rover simulator with live telemetry.

The project’s intended benefit is to make planetary exploration data easier to understand and use in a mission-planning experience. By combining route choices, scientific stops, EVA time considerations, mission notes, and planetary time in one hub, it helps users explore how an astronaut might prepare for a surface walk.

The project includes ESP32 firmware, alongside a web-based hub built with technologies represented in the project repository, including C++, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Python. The existing firmware uses Wi-Fi and HTTPS; the documentation did not find an implemented LoRa connection, measured power consumption or battery life, or physical-board validation. Adapting the NASA data simulation for low power ESP32 class hardware and LoRa connected field nodes is a future direction, not a current capability.

Our team considered data provenance, the difference between a challenge requirement and a formal NASA standard, the assumptions and units used in EVA planning, offline behavior, privacy, licensing, and the limits of what has actually been tested. The Mars time documentation references NASA GISS Mars24 and checks its published example, but the exact clock calculation used by the new hub still needs verification. Likewise, some module behavior and integration tests remain to be confirmed.
